job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Rafael Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a rented house near campus in Columbus, Ohio with two guys from my church. Weekdays I'm in class for my master's in finance, and on Saturdays I detail cars at a dealership, washing and vacuuming from seven to four. Sunday is church in the morning, then I call my fiancée Hannah, who's finishing a nursing assistant course three hours away.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me how you got to this point.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I grew up in Marion, a small town north of here. My dad owns a hardware store that's been in the family 40 years and is barely hanging on, so there's no money coming from home, and I'd never ask. I did a finance bachelor's, passed, no internship, because I worked in the store every summer. I owe about 62,000 dollars. I'm doing the master's because Hannah and I want to marry next summer, and I need to show I can provide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good. Hard work and honest dealing still count for something, and the hype will pass, like most of it does. I'd say it at church and over the counter at Dad's store, where people ask me about it all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pressure's the same as now, and it isn't small. I've got 62,000 in loans and few finance jobs open in the area, mostly in Columbus, and everyone I know is applying for them. I'd still be waiting on a first job offer with a wedding on the calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, send 40 applications to banks and insurance companies, and push to meet a few people at the church who work in finance. I'd keep the car detailing on Saturdays, work the register at Dad's store when I visit, and pay 200 a month on the loan. I wouldn't take any big risk with the wedding coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, honestly. I trust the Lord and my work, but I wake up some nights counting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a wedding next summer. How does that change the pressure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad that he should keep the store as long as it's paying for itself, and I'd offer to do his books on weekends. He doesn't want my help, because he thinks it's his burden, but I'd offer anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your father about the store?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes everything feel urgent. I don't want a wedding on credit cards, and Hannah's family is watching to see if I can provide. It's a lot of weight on one first job.

say: I'd say **hard work** and honest dealing still count for something.
I'd say it at church and at my dad's store.
think: The pressure is the **same as now**: 62,000 in loans and few finance jobs open.
I'd be waiting on a first offer with a **wedding** on the calendar.
do: Send **40 applications** to banks and insurers.
Keep the Saturday car detailing and pay 200 a month on the loan.
feel: **Tense**, trusting the Lord but counting at night.

fieldNote: The **wedding** converts a quiet world into an urgent one.
His father's store means **no cash** from home and a family worry.
Church ties are his real **job network**.

steps.text: Send 40 applications to banks and insurance companies
Keep detailing cars on Saturdays for the dealership
Keep the wedding small and paid in cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we shouldn't fear it, but we shouldn't brush it off either. The people who work hard and keep learning will be fine. And families need to stick together while it settles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. The jobs I'm aiming at, like junior analyst at a bank, are about spreadsheets, checks and summaries, which is what the software does. If a bank can hire three people instead of ten, I'm competing with a lot of smart people for very few seats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools more, since a few of my classmates already do, and I'd learn the specific ones banks use. I'd widen my search to local credit unions and insurance agencies, where a person talking to customers still matters. I'd keep the wedding date, but plan it small, 50 guests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but determined. I'd rather be busy than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hannah about the wedding plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hannah would say we'll manage, as she always does. I'd tell her we might have to move to a bigger city for the first job, and she's open to that if her nursing work travels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of finance would you expect to stay in human hands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The relationships. A banker who's known the farmer for 20 years, a person who sits across from a customer. A machine can crunch the numbers, but people trust people.

say: I'd say we shouldn't fear it or brush it off, and hard workers who keep **learning** will be fine.
I'd say families must stick together.
think: Junior analyst work is **spreadsheets and summaries**, which software does.
A bank hiring three instead of ten means few seats.
do: Use AI tools more and learn the ones **banks use**.
Widen the search to **credit unions** and insurance agencies.
Keep the wedding date but plan it small, **50 guests**.
feel: **Anxious but determined**, busy rather than worried.
S1.quote: A machine can crunch the numbers, but people trust people.
fieldNote: Steady adopter: starts using AI because **classmates** do.
Turns to **relationship** jobs like credit unions.
The wedding date holds but the **budget** shrinks to 50 guests, which he accepts without complaint.

steps.text: Learn the AI tools banks use for junior analysis
Apply to credit unions and insurance agencies near Columbus
Plan a small wedding with 50 guests

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll get through it if we stay close and work hard, and I'd quietly ask the government to slow down and give people time. I don't like handouts, but if everyone's job goes at once, people need help to eat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be frightened. Finance is thinking work and two years isn't enough to turn my life around. I'd be 26, in debt by 62,000, and I'm not sure I'd ever have a job where I use what I studied.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the wedding off a year, which would break my heart. I'd take any work I could find, hands-on if need be, like working full-time at Dad's store or at the dealership, since robots take about three more years. And I'd keep the loan payments, because defaulting would ruin me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd pray, and I'd pace the kitchen at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hannah and her parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Hannah and her parents the truth: I'd want to marry her, but I wouldn't promise a house. I'd say I'm willing to work any hand job to keep her safe. Her father would respect that, even if he's disappointed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about your dad's store?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work there full-time and try to stretch it for as long as it pays. A hardware store has something a screen doesn't: you can fix a leaking pipe with what you pick off the shelf.

say: I'd say we'll get through it if we **stay close** and work hard.
I'd quietly ask the government to slow down and give people time.
think: Two years isn't enough to turn my life around, with **62,000** in debt.
I might never have a job using what I studied.
do: Work full-time at **Dad's store** or the dealership.
feel: **Alarmed**, praying and pacing the kitchen at night.
S2.quote: A hardware store has something a screen doesn't: you can fix a leaking pipe with what you pick off the shelf.
fieldNote: The **wedding delay** is his worst loss, more than the job.
Falls back on **hands-on** work in his father's store.
Honest with Hannah's parents: **no promise** of a house.

steps.text: Put the wedding off for a year
Work full-time at Dad's hardware store
Keep the Saturday dealership shifts as long as they last
Keep making the loan payments to avoid default

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to prepare if you start now. I'd tell my friends to learn a skill and save, and I'd tell the church to look out for people who lose their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be nervous but I'd see a path. Five years gets us married, gets me a first job, and puts a good dent in the loan. By 2031 I'd be 29, with a child maybe, and I'd need work that's still around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a first job in the city for two years, then see what's changed. I'd marry next summer as planned, and keep it small. I'd send 300 a month to the loan, and I'd learn the AI tools my employer uses. I'd also help Dad shift his store to online ordering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steady. Five years feels like a storm warning when you've still got time to board up the windows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years let you do for the wedding and the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the first job is only in Columbus, I'd stay. If it's in Chicago, I'd go, but only if Hannah can get nursing work there. We'd ask both our families and decide together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether to move to a big city?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years we can marry, start a home, and not be panicking. With two years I wouldn't know whether to start a family.

I'd tell the church to look out for people who lose jobs.
think: I'd see a path: married, a **first job** and a dent in the loan.
By 2031 I'd need work that's still around.
do: Take a first job in the **city** for two years.

feel: **Anxious but steady**, like a storm warning with time to board up the windows.

steps.text: Take a first finance job in a city for two years
Marry next summer with a small ceremony
Send 300 a month to the student loan
Learn the AI tools my first employer uses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, a decade is a long time and people shouldn't panic. I'd say hard work and good character will still matter, and communities should help each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be mostly fine. By 34 I'd have a job, a home, probably two kids, and the loan mostly paid. My worry would be the town I grew up in, where jobs would vanish and nobody would have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a first job, work hard, pay off the loan in eight years, and learn new tools as they come. Hannah and I would buy a small house. I'd stay involved in the church and maybe start a local finance club to teach young people how to manage money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. Almost normal, with debt and a mortgage as the usual pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach your future children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To be useful to people, to earn what you get, and not to be too proud to learn. Machines can do a lot, but they can't take care of your neighbours when they're hurting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you still worry about with a decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marion. I worry that small towns get left behind when the work moves to big companies and machines. Ten years is enough to help, but someone has to start.

say: I'd say a decade is long and people shouldn't **panic**.
I'd say hard work and good character will still matter.
think: I'd be mostly fine at 34 with a **job, a home** and kids.
I'd worry about my hometown, where jobs would vanish with no plan.
do: Take a first job and pay the loan off in **eight years**.
Buy a small house with Hannah.
Start a local **finance club** teaching young people money skills.
feel: **Better**, almost normal, with debt and a mortgage as usual pressure.
S4.quote: Machines can do a lot, but they can't take care of your neighbours when they're hurting.
fieldNote: A decade restores a **normal life** plan with the usual debts.
His worry is **Marion**, his hometown, more than himself.
Community teaching is his way to **give back**.

steps.text: Take a first finance job and work hard

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2-year one, because it'd break the wedding plans and I'd have no time. What would help is time, work that pays a fair wage, and a community that stays together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what keeps me going. It's Hannah, my faith and the memory of my dad's store. I want to be as honest as my dad's hardware store has always been.

headlineQuote: I want to be as honest as my dad's hardware store has always been.
portrait: Rafael is a **24-year-old** finance master's student in Columbus, owing 62,000 dollars, with a wedding planned for next summer.
He is **traditional**: values work, faith, community and family, and prefers help from neighbours over handouts.
He is **steady** with AI, starting to use it because classmates do and learning the tools banks use.
His mood is **anxious** in most worlds and alarmed at 2028, when the wedding itself is at risk.
His father's **hardware store** is a family burden and a model of honest work.
biggestWorry: Rafael fears **2028** most, because it would break the wedding plans and leave no time.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **time**, fair-paying work and a community that stays together.
